title: Aperture and depth of field
summary: The aperture controls light and how much of the scene is sharp at the same time. It is the control that most changes how a photograph feels.
keywords: exposure aperture depth of field exposure-and-settings
body: The aperture is a ring of overlapping blades inside the lens that opens and closes to change the size of the hole light passes through. It does two things at once, which is what makes it the most interesting of the three controls. The numbering Apertures are written as s — f/1.4, f/2, f/2.8, f/4, f/5.6, f/8, f/11, f/16 — and the sequence looks arbitrary until you know where it comes from. The number is a ratio: the lens's divided by the width of the opening. Because it is a division, a smaller number means a wider opening . The steps go up by a factor of √2, which halves the area of the hole each time and so halves the light. Each step is one . The ratio is why f/4 admits the same light on any lens, wide or telephoto. That is the entire point of the system, and it is worth the awkward numbering. The second job A wider opening also narrows the band of distance that comes out sharp — the . Wide open, a portrait has sharp eyes and a background dissolved into . Stopped down to f/16, a landscape is sharp from the rocks at your feet to the hills behind. Three things make depth of field shallower: 1. A wider aperture. 2. A longer focal length. 3. Standing closer to the subject. They compo

title: The letters on the mode dial
summary: P, A, S and M are not difficulty levels. Each hands you a different control and does the arithmetic on the rest.
body: The mode dial is not a difficulty ladder with automatic at one end and expertise at the other. Each mode hands you one control and works out the others. What each one does Mode You set Camera sets P — Program Nothing; you can shift the pairing Aperture and shutter A or Av — Aperture priority Shutter S or Tv — Shutter priority Aperture M — Manual Both Nothing sits outside this and can be automatic or fixed in any of them. Canon writes Av and Tv where most others write A and S. Same modes, different labels. Choosing between them The useful question is: which control does this photograph depend on? Aperture priority when is what matters — portraits, landscapes, anything where the background is part of the decision. This is what most working photographers leave their cameras in. Shutter priority when movement is what matters — sport, children, running water. You are saying "whatever else happens, do not go slower than this". Manual when the light is constant and you want it to stop changing between frames, or when the scene keeps fooling the meter and you are tired of arguing with it via . Program when you want the camera to get you something usable while you think about where to stand

title: Files, cards and what to keep
summary: RAW or JPEG, which memory card to buy, and the backup habit that stops one failure from costing you everything.
body: The least interesting part of photography, and the one that costs people the most when they get it wrong. RAW or JPEG Two ways the camera can save what the sensor recorded. A is finished. The camera has applied its own white balance, contrast and sharpening, thrown away what it did not need, and compressed the result into a small file anyone can open. A file is the sensor's data with the interpretation left off. It is not really a picture yet — it needs software to become one — but it holds far more of the original range. RAW JPEG Room to correct Large Small File size Several times bigger Small Ready to share No Yes White balance Changeable afterwards Baked in The practical rule: shoot RAW when the light is difficult or the photograph matters, JPEG when neither is true. Most cameras will record both simultaneously, which costs card space and settles the argument. RAW is not a magic recovery tool. It buys perhaps a stop of latitude at each end — real, but far less than getting the exposure right in the first place. Memory cards Two numbers matter, and only one of them usually does. Capacity is straightforward. Speed matters if you shoot bursts or video; for single photographs almost

title: Focus, and what it is for
summary: Autofocus is very good at focusing accurately on the wrong thing. Deciding what should be sharp is the part it cannot do for you.
body: A lens forms a sharp image at exactly one distance. Focusing is choosing that distance. Everything nearer or further is technically not in focus. is the band either side where it is close enough that nobody notices — but there is still only one plane that is genuinely sharp. The part the camera cannot do Modern autofocus is fast and accurate. What it cannot do is know which part of the scene you care about. Left to itself, a camera tends to pick whatever is nearest, or highest in contrast, or in the middle of the frame. For a portrait against a busy street that is often a lamppost. The fix is to choose the focus point yourself rather than letting the camera choose. On most cameras this means switching from an automatic area mode to single point, and then moving that point onto the thing that matters. For a portrait, the thing that matters is the eye nearest the camera. If the eyes are sharp, a photograph forgives a great deal elsewhere; if they are not, nothing else rescues it. Single and continuous Two modes, and the choice is about whether the distance is changing. Single focuses once and locks. Right for anything still: a landscape, a building, a person sitting down. Continuous

title: Holding the camera steady
summary: Most photographs that beginners call out of focus are not. They are blurred by the photographer's own movement, and that has a specific cure.
body: Pick up a camera and it moves. Your pulse moves it, your breathing moves it, and the act of pressing the button moves it. If the shutter is open long enough for that movement to matter, the whole frame smears. This is , and it is probably the single most common reason a beginner's photographs are not sharp. Telling it apart from the alternatives Three different faults look like "blurry" and have three different cures, so it is worth learning to tell them apart. What you see What it is What fixes it Everything soft, including still things Camera shake Faster shutter, or support Subject smeared, background sharp Faster shutter Something else sharp instead Missed Focus on the right thing The tell for camera shake is that things which were definitely not moving — a wall, a table — are soft as well. How fast is fast enough The rule of thumb is the : use a shutter speed at least as fast as one over the . 24mm lens → 1/25s or faster 50mm lens → 1/50s or faster 200mm lens → 1/200s or faster A longer lens magnifies your movement exactly as much as it magnifies the subject, which is why it demands more. It is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee. It assumes decent technique and no stabilisation,

title: ISO and noise
summary: ISO buys brightness when there is not enough light, and pays for it with noise. Knowing when that trade is worth it is the skill.
body: describes how strongly the camera amplifies what the sensor collected. Doubling it — 100 to 200, 200 to 400 — buys one of brightness. It is the only one of the three controls that does not change how much light actually arrives. It turns up the volume on what did. Why that matters Amplifying a signal amplifies whatever else is in it. The result is : a speckled texture that shows first and worst in the shadows, because that is where the signal was weakest. This is why ISO is the control to reach for last. Aperture and shutter speed collect more light; ISO makes do with less. Raising ISO does not create noise so much as reveal it. The same noise was always there — the amplification just brings it up alongside the picture. When to raise it anyway Constantly. The alternative to a noisy photograph is usually a blurred one or no photograph at all, and noise is by far the least bad of those. The order that works: 1. Open the aperture as far as the depth of field allows. 2. Slow the shutter as far as the subject and your hands allow. 3. Then raise the ISO to cover the rest. If steps one and two are exhausted and the photograph is still dark, ISO is not a compromise — it is the answer. Unde

title: Metering, and why it lies
summary: Your camera's meter assumes every scene averages to mid-grey. Knowing when that assumption fails explains most automatic exposure mistakes.
body: Your camera measures the light before it chooses an exposure. That measurement rests on one assumption, and understanding the assumption explains nearly every automatic exposure mistake you will see. The assumption A meter assumes that whatever it is pointed at averages out to — a tone reflecting about 18% of the light falling on it. Point a camera at anything and it will choose an exposure that renders that thing as middle grey. Point it at a white wall and it gives you a grey wall. Point it at a black cat and it gives you a grey cat. For most scenes this works, because most scenes contain a mixture of light and dark that genuinely does average out near the middle. Where it fails Two situations, and they fail in opposite directions. A bright background. A person photographed against a bright sky: the meter reads mostly sky, decides the scene is very bright, and cuts the exposure. The sky comes out correct and the face comes out dark. A uniformly bright or dark scene. A snow field is not mid grey — it is snow. The meter reads it, renders it as mid grey, and hands you a photograph of dirty slush. A black cat filling the frame comes out grey for the same reason. The second case is th

title: Shutter speed
summary: How long the sensor is exposed decides whether movement is frozen or smeared. It is the most visible of the three controls.
body: The shutter is a curtain in front of the sensor. Shutter speed is how long it stays open, and it is the control whose effect is easiest to see. The numbers Written as fractions of a second: 1/1000, 1/500, 1/250, and so on down to whole seconds. Each step in that sequence halves or doubles the time, and so halves or doubles the light — one . The printed numbers are rounded. A camera marked 1/125 is really giving you 1/128; the sequence is powers of two underneath, which is what makes the stops exact. Freezing and smearing Anything that moves while the shutter is open records in more than one place, and that reads as a smear along the direction of travel. Subject Roughly enough to freeze A person standing, small movements 1/60 Someone walking 1/250 Someone running 1/500 A cyclist or a car at speed 1/1000 or faster Three things push those numbers up: a faster subject, a closer subject, and a longer lens. All three amount to the same thing — how quickly the subject crosses the frame. Movement across your view smears far more than movement towards you. A car driving past needs a much faster shutter than the same car driving at you. Blur on purpose A smear is not a fault unless you did n

title: The exposure triangle
summary: Three controls decide how bright a photograph is, and each one changes something else as well. That trade-off is the whole of exposure.
body: Three controls decide how bright a photograph is. Any of them will brighten or darken it, and each one also changes something no other control can. That second effect is why the choice matters. If brightness were all that mattered, you could pick any of them at random. Everything is measured in stops A is a doubling or halving of light. It is the unit that makes the three controls interchangeable. Control One stop more light 1/500 → 1/250 f/8 → f/5.6 ISO 200 → ISO 400 Because they are the same size, they trade evenly. Give up one stop on the shutter and take it back on the aperture and the brightness is identical. Thinking in stops rather than in numbers is most of learning exposure. The numbers are irregular and awkward; the stops are all the same size. Reciprocal exposures Because a stop given up on one control can be taken back on another, many different combinations produce exactly the same brightness: Aperture Shutter ISO Brightness f/2.8 1/1000 100 identical f/4 1/500 100 identical f/5.6 1/250 100 identical f/5.6 1/1000 400 identical These are not the same photograph. The first has a soft background and freezes movement. The third has more in focus. The fourth freezes movemen

title: What a camera actually does
summary: A camera collects light for a measured moment and records it. Everything else is a way of controlling how much, and for how long.
body: Strip away the menus and a camera is a light tight box with a hole in one end and a sensor at the other. Everything it does is a way of controlling how much light comes through that hole, for how long, and how strongly the result is amplified. Light in, picture out Light reflects off whatever you are photographing, passes through the lens, and lands on the sensor. The sensor counts how much arrives at each point and turns that into numbers. Too little light and the numbers are small and unreliable, which looks like a dark, muddy photograph. Too much and they hit their ceiling, which looks like blank white where detail used to be. Getting a usable amount is called exposure, and there are exactly three ways to change it. The three controls The is a ring of blades inside the lens. Opening it wider lets more light through. The is how long the sensor is uncovered. Longer means more light. The is how much the signal is amplified afterwards. Higher means a brighter result from the same light. That is the whole system. Every mode dial, every automatic setting, every piece of advice you will read is about choosing between these three. Each one changes brightness, and each one has a second e

title: Aperture
summary: The adjustable opening inside a lens that controls how much light reaches the sensor, and how much of the scene is sharp.

title: Bokeh
summary: The quality of the out-of-focus areas in a photograph — not how much blur there is, but what it looks like.

title: Camera shake
summary: Blur across the whole frame caused by the photographer's own movement during the exposure.

title: Clipping
summary: Where a photograph has gone to pure white or pure black, losing all detail in that area permanently.

title: Crop factor
summary: The number describing how much smaller a sensor is than full-frame, and therefore how much narrower the view through the same lens.

title: Depth of field
summary: The band of distance, in front of and behind the focus point, that comes out acceptably sharp in a photograph.

title: Exposure compensation
summary: A control that tells the camera its meter reading is wrong, and by how many stops, without leaving automatic mode.

title: Exposure triangle
summary: The relationship between aperture, shutter speed and ISO — the three controls that together decide how bright a photograph is.

title: f-number
summary: The number that describes an aperture, written f/2 or f/8. It is the focal length divided by the width of the opening.

title: Focal length
summary: A lens's angle of view, measured in millimetres. Shorter takes in more of the scene; longer magnifies a narrower slice of it.

title: Focus
summary: Setting the lens so that a chosen distance is rendered sharply.

title: Full-frame
summary: A sensor the same size as a frame of 35mm film, 36 by 24 millimetres. The reference format most photography writing assumes.

title: Histogram
summary: A graph of how many pixels fall at each brightness, from black on the left to white on the right.

title: ISO
summary: How strongly the camera amplifies the signal from its sensor. Higher values let you shoot in less light, at the cost of visible noise.

title: JPEG
summary: A finished, compressed image file produced by the camera from the sensor data, ready to share.

title: Metering
summary: How a camera measures the light in a scene in order to choose an exposure — and the assumption that makes it get some scenes wrong.

title: Middle grey
summary: The tone a light meter assumes a scene averages out to — a grey reflecting about 18% of the light falling on it.

title: Motion blur
summary: The smear left when a subject moves across the frame while the shutter is open.

title: Noise
summary: The speckled texture that appears in a photograph, most visibly in the shadows, when the sensor's signal is amplified.

title: RAW
summary: An image file holding the sensor's data more or less as recorded, before the camera turns it into a picture.

title: Reciprocal rule
summary: A rule of thumb: to hand-hold sharply, use a shutter speed at least as fast as one over the focal length.

title: Shutter speed
summary: How long the sensor is exposed to light, usually a fraction of a second. It decides whether movement is frozen or blurred.

title: Stop
summary: A doubling or halving of light. Every exposure control is measured in stops, which is what lets them trade against each other.

title: Zone system
summary: A way of describing brightness in eleven steps, from pure black to paper white, each one stop apart.

title: Should I shoot in manual or aperture priority?
summary: Aperture priority, most of the time. It is faster than manual and the camera's meter is right more often than not. Manual earns its place when the light is cons
body: Aperture priority, most of the time. It is faster than manual and the camera's meter is right more often than not. Manual earns its place when the light is constant and you want it to stop changing between frames, or when the scene keeps fooling the meter. Neither of those is most photographs.

title: Can I clean a lens with my shirt or a glasses cloth?
summary: Not with a shirt — fabric carries grit, and grit is what actually scratches coatings. A clean microfibre cloth is fine for smears. Blow the loose dust off first
body: Not with a shirt — fabric carries grit, and grit is what actually scratches coatings. A clean microfibre cloth is fine for smears. Blow the loose dust off first, because wiping it is how a dusty lens becomes a scratched one.

title: Do I need a full-frame camera?
summary: No. A smaller sensor is not a worse sensor; it captures a smaller part of the image the lens projects, so the view is narrower. What it does mean is that advice
body: No. A smaller sensor is not a worse sensor; it captures a smaller part of the image the lens projects, so the view is narrower. What it does mean is that advice written for needs translating. A 50mm lens on an APS C camera frames like a 75mm lens would on full frame — that is the .

title: Is it better to underexpose and brighten later?
summary: No. Brightening a dark file amplifies the same noise that raising the ISO would have, usually with less information to work with. Protect the highlights, becaus
body: No. Brightening a dark file amplifies the same noise that raising the ISO would have, usually with less information to work with. Protect the highlights, because at the bright end is permanent — but do not deliberately underexpose beyond that.

title: How slow can I hand-hold before things go soft?
summary: The starting point is the : one over the . A 50mm lens wants 1/50s or faster, a 200mm lens wants 1/200s. Stabilisation buys two or three stops beyond that. Tech
body: The starting point is the : one over the . A 50mm lens wants 1/50s or faster, a 200mm lens wants 1/200s. Stabilisation buys two or three stops beyond that. Technique — elbows in, breathe out, lean on something — is worth about one more, and costs nothing.

title: How often should I back up my photographs?
summary: The same day you take them. The gap between shooting and copying is where losses happen. One copy is not a backup, and two copies on the same computer are not e
body: The same day you take them. The gap between shooting and copying is where losses happen. One copy is not a backup, and two copies on the same computer are not either — they fail together. The workable minimum is your computer plus somewhere that is not your computer.

title: How often should I clean my sensor?
summary: When you can see the marks, and not before. Photograph a plain bright surface at f/16 and look for dark specks in the same place in every frame. Most dust never
body: When you can see the marks, and not before. Photograph a plain bright surface at f/16 and look for dark specks in the same place in every frame. Most dust never shows at normal apertures. Cleaning carries some risk and doing it unnecessarily is the more common mistake.

title: Should I shoot RAW or JPEG?
summary: when the light is difficult or the photograph matters, because it survives correction far better. when neither is true and you want something you can share stra
body: when the light is difficult or the photograph matters, because it survives correction far better. when neither is true and you want something you can share straight away. Most cameras will record both at once, which costs card space and settles the question.

title: What camera should I buy to learn on?
summary: Almost any camera with manual controls. The three controls behave identically on a twelve year old entry level body and on the most expensive one made, and it i
body: Almost any camera with manual controls. The three controls behave identically on a twelve year old entry level body and on the most expensive one made, and it is the controls you are learning. Spend the money on a lens with a wide maximum aperture instead — a 50mm f/1.8 costs very little and does more for what your photographs look like than a better body would.

title: What ISO is too high?
summary: Whichever one your eyes object to, on your camera, at the size you actually look at photographs. Published figures are less useful than twenty minutes of testin
body: Whichever one your eyes object to, on your camera, at the size you actually look at photographs. Published figures are less useful than twenty minutes of testing your own body. The more useful principle: a noisy photograph of something beats a clean photograph of nothing. When the aperture is wide open and the shutter is as slow as you can hold, raise the without agonising.

title: Why are my photos blurry?
summary: Three different faults look the same and have different cures. If everything is soft, including things that were not moving, it is — use a faster shutter speed
body: Three different faults look the same and have different cures. If everything is soft, including things that were not moving, it is — use a faster shutter speed or rest the camera on something. If only the subject is smeared and the background is sharp, it is — the subject moved, so use a faster shutter. If something else in the frame is perfectly sharp, the focus went to the wrong place. Choose the focus point yourself rather than letting the camera pick.

title: Why does snow come out grey?
summary: Because your camera's meter assumes every scene averages out to , and exposes to make it so. Snow is not mid grey. The fix is , usually +1 to +2 stops. Changing
body: Because your camera's meter assumes every scene averages out to , and exposes to make it so. Snow is not mid grey. The fix is , usually +1 to +2 stops. Changing the metering mode does not help here — when the whole frame is snow, it does not matter how much of it the camera measures.

title: Cleaning a lens without scratching it
summary: Most lens damage happens during cleaning, not before it. The order of operations matters more than what you clean with.
body: Front elements are coated, and coatings scratch. Almost all the damage people do to lenses happens while cleaning them, which makes the order of operations more important than the products. The principle: remove loose dust before anything touches the glass. A grain of sand under a cloth is sandpaper. Blow the dust off first Use a hand blower — a rubber bulb, not canned air, which can spit propellant onto the glass. Hold the lens face down so what you dislodge falls away rather than settling back. This alone deals with most of what is on a lens most of the time. Brush what the blower missed A soft lens brush, used lightly, takes off anything still clinging. Do not use it on a lens you have already wetted, and do not touch the bristles with your fingers — the oils transfer. Only now, wipe For fingerprints and smears, a drop of lens fluid on a microfibre cloth or a lens tissue. Put the fluid on the cloth, never directly on the lens, where it can run into the barrel. Work from the centre outward in a spiral, with light pressure. Finish with a dry part of the cloth. What not to use Shirts, sleeves and tissues — all carry grit. Canned air — can spit propellant and drive dust into the bar

title: Storing a camera between uses
summary: Batteries, humidity and the slow damage that happens to kit left in a bag. What actually matters and what does not.
body: Cameras are more often damaged by sitting still than by being used. Three things do the damage, and all three are cheap to avoid. Humidity, and fungus Lens fungus grows in still, damp air and etches the coatings permanently. Once it is established the lens usually needs professional attention, and sometimes is not worth saving. It needs moisture and darkness. A camera bag in a cupboard in a humid climate is close to ideal for it. Keep kit somewhere with moving air rather than sealed in a bag. Silica gel in the bag, dried out or replaced periodically. In a genuinely humid climate, a dry cabinet is worth the money. Let equipment see daylight occasionally; fungus does not like it. Batteries Lithium batteries do not like being stored full, and they do not like being stored empty. For long storage, leave them around half charged. Take them out of the camera if it will be months, so a slow drain cannot deep discharge them. Store them somewhere cool. Heat ages them faster than use does. Pressure and shape A bag crushed under other things will eventually stress a lens mount or a screen. Store bodies with a lens or a cap fitted, and do not leave heavy items resting on a bag long term. title: When to clean your sensor, and when to leave it alone
summary: Sensor dust is easy to diagnose and easy to over-treat. How to tell whether it is worth touching at all.
body: Sensor dust shows as dark specks in exactly the same place in every photograph. That repetition is the diagnosis: a mark that moves is on your screen, and a mark that stays is on the sensor. Find out whether you have any Set the smallest your lens offers — f/16 or f/22 — and photograph something plain and bright. A white wall, an overcast sky, a sheet of paper. Look at the result at full size. Dust shows at small apertures and disappears at wide ones, which is why it is invisible in most photographs and obvious in a landscape at f/16. If you cannot see marks in that test, you do not have a problem worth solving. Cleaning carries some risk, and cleaning unnecessarily is the more common mistake. Try the camera's own cleaning first Almost every camera has a sensor cleaning routine that vibrates the filter in front of the sensor. It is free, carries no risk, and shifts a useful proportion of what lands there. Run it a few times before doing anything else. Then a blower, and nothing else Lock the mirror up or enter sensor cleaning mode, hold the camera face down, and use a hand blower without letting the tip enter the chamber. Do not use canned air. title: Focus on the nearest eye
summary: When depth of field is shallow, which eye you focus on is the difference between a portrait that works and one that does not.
body: At a wide aperture, the band of sharpness in a portrait can be shallower than the distance between someone's two eyes. Focus on the one nearest the camera. Viewers look at eyes first and forgive softness almost everywhere else — but a portrait with the far eye sharp and the near one soft reads as a mistake, even to people who could not say why.

title: Half-press before you commit
summary: The half-press tells you what the camera is about to do. Reading it takes a second and prevents most automatic exposure surprises.
body: Half pressing the shutter makes the camera focus and meter, and shows you both — the focus point it chose, and the shutter speed and aperture it intends to use. Two things are worth reading in that second. Is the focus point on the thing you care about? And is the shutter speed fast enough for the lens you are holding, by the ? Most automatic exposure disappointments are visible there, before the photograph exists.

title: Take the boring frame first
summary: Get one safe photograph before you experiment. It costs nothing and it means you leave with something.
body: When something is happening, take the obvious, safe, correctly exposed frame before you start trying anything. It costs one press. Then experiment freely — slow the shutter, open the aperture, move — knowing that if none of it works you still have the photograph. The habit matters most exactly when the moment will not repeat.

title: The cheapest upgrade is a wider aperture
summary: A 50mm f/1.8 costs less than almost any accessory and changes what your photographs look like more than a new camera body would.
body: Kit zooms are usually f/3.5 at the wide end and f/5.6 at the long end. A basic 50mm prime is f/1.8, which is between two and three s wider. That buys two things at once: enough extra light to keep shooting after the zoom has run out, and shallow enough to separate a subject from its background. It is almost always the least expensive lens a manufacturer makes, and it will do more for what your photographs look like than a newer body would.

title: Freeze the pendulum
summary: The bob is swinging past a ruled backdrop. Catch it sharply as it passes through the centre, where it is moving fastest — without over- or under-exposing the sh
body: The bob is swinging past a ruled backdrop. Catch it sharply as it passes through the centre, where it is moving fastest — without over- or under-exposing the shot.

title: Show the swing
summary: Now the opposite. Let the bob blur across at least a couple of the backdrop's rules, so the photograph says the pendulum was moving — while keeping the exposure
body: Now the opposite. Let the bob blur across at least a couple of the backdrop's rules, so the photograph says the pendulum was moving — while keeping the exposure correct.

title: Steady in the hand
summary: A still life indoors, hand-held. Nothing is moving, but you are. Find a shutter speed that exposes correctly without the camera's own shake softening the pictur
body: A still life indoors, hand-held. Nothing is moving, but you are. Find a shutter speed that exposes correctly without the camera's own shake softening the picture.

title: Separate the subject
summary: Focus is on the second marker. Open the lens far enough that the furthest marker dissolves into a soft wash, so the eye goes straight to the subject — and keep
body: Focus is on the second marker. Open the lens far enough that the furthest marker dissolves into a soft wash, so the eye goes straight to the subject — and keep the exposure right.

title: Keep it all sharp
summary: The opposite problem. Stop the lens down until even the furthest marker is readable, front to back, without losing the exposure.
body: The opposite problem. Stop the lens down until even the furthest marker is readable, front to back, without losing the exposure.

title: Just enough separation
summary: Flat, dull light this time. Soften the background enough that the subject stands clear, but not so much that the scene loses its sense of depth — and expose it
body: Flat, dull light this time. Soften the background enough that the subject stands clear, but not so much that the scene loses its sense of depth — and expose it correctly.

title: Find the light
summary: Window light only, and the shutter is already as slow as you can hold steady. Raise the sensor's sensitivity until the still life is properly exposed.
body: Window light only, and the shutter is already as slow as you can hold steady. Raise the sensor's sensitivity until the still life is properly exposed.

title: As clean as you can
summary: Same room, but now noise matters. Expose it correctly at the lowest sensitivity that will do the job — anything higher is grain you did not need to accept.
body: Same room, but now noise matters. Expose it correctly at the lowest sensitivity that will do the job — anything higher is grain you did not need to accept.

title: Last light of the day
summary: Evening now, and two stops darker. Get a usable exposure — this time the sensitivity has to go somewhere you would rather it did not.
body: Evening now, and two stops darker. Get a usable exposure — this time the sensitivity has to go somewhere you would rather it did not.

title: Frozen and separated
summary: Catch the bob sharp as it crosses the centre, and throw the distant backdrop out of focus at the same time. The shutter decides one, the aperture the other, and
body: Catch the bob sharp as it crosses the centre, and throw the distant backdrop out of focus at the same time. The shutter decides one, the aperture the other, and between them they have to leave the exposure right.

title: Sharp throughout
summary: Everything sharp from the nearest marker to the furthest, at a shutter speed you could hold in the hand. A narrow aperture and a fast shutter both want light, a
body: Everything sharp from the nearest marker to the furthest, at a shutter speed you could hold in the hand. A narrow aperture and a fast shutter both want light, and there is only so much of it.

title: A sense of movement
summary: Let the bob smear to show it was moving, but keep the backdrop crisp so there is something to measure that movement against. A slow shutter and a sharp backgrou
body: Let the bob smear to show it was moving, but keep the backdrop crisp so there is something to measure that movement against. A slow shutter and a sharp background pull in opposite directions.

title: Full manual
summary: Everything is yours now. Freeze the bob, soften the backdrop, expose it correctly, and keep the sensitivity low enough that the picture stays clean.
body: Everything is yours now. Freeze the bob, soften the backdrop, expose it correctly, and keep the sensitivity low enough that the picture stays clean.

title: The whole room
summary: Indoors and hand-held, with depth to hold and not much light to hold it with. Sharp front to back, steady in the hand, correctly exposed, and as clean as you ca
body: Indoors and hand-held, with depth to hold and not much light to hold it with. Sharp front to back, steady in the hand, correctly exposed, and as clean as you can manage.

body: Dull light, and a portrait to make. Separate the subject from the background, hold the camera steady, expose it properly, and keep the noise down. Every control matters and none of them is free.

body: The camera is exposing this one. A bright sky fills most of the frame and the figure is in its own shadow — see what the camera makes of that, then get the figure exposed properly.

title: Why is the snow grey?

body: Nothing is backlit and there is no bright background to blame. The scene is evenly lit, every metering mode agrees — and the photograph is still wrong. Work out why, and fix it.
